summary.text: Bacteria are a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms, mostly free-living and often made of one cell a few micrometres long.
They live in the air, soil, water, acidic hot springs and radioactive waste, and they recycle nutrients and fix nitrogen from the atmosphere.
Most bacteria in and on the human body are harmless or made so by the immune system, while some species cause diseases such as cholera and tuberculosis.

items.prompt: Which feature separates a bacterial cell from the cell of an animal?

options.label: A nucleus that surrounds its chromosomes
Many membrane-bound organelles inside
Circular chromosomes and no nucleus
Straight, rod-shaped chromosomes only

items.explain: Unlike animal and other eukaryote cells, bacterial cells have circular chromosomes, no nucleus and rarely any membrane-bound organelles.

items.prompt: A gardener asks what the tiny single-celled life in soil actually does for the garden. What is a good answer?

options.label: It recycles nutrients and fixes nitrogen from the air
It only feeds on dead matter and adds nothing back
It keeps nitrogen from the air from reaching plants
It stays out of soil and water, so it plays no part

items.explain: Bacteria play a vital role in the nutrient cycle by recycling nutrients and fixing atmospheric nitrogen.

items.prompt: How do extremophile bacteria support life around a deep-sea hydrothermal vent?

options.label: They carry sunlight down from the water's surface
They remove all the dissolved compounds from the water
They eat the larger animals that gather around the vent
They turn dissolved compounds like hydrogen sulphide into energy

items.explain: Extremophile bacteria convert dissolved compounds such as hydrogen sulphide and methane to energy, providing the nutrients that sustain life there.

items.prompt: A textbook once grouped all prokaryotes under one name. What changed that view?

options.label: Bacteria were found to have a nucleus like animals
Prokaryotes were found to be two very different groups
Bacteria were reclassified as plants called fission fungi
Prokaryotes were found to have no shared ancestor

items.explain: The 1990s discovery that prokaryotes consist of two very different groups that evolved from an ancient common ancestor led to the domains Bacteria and Archaea.

items.prompt: The word bacteria comes from a Greek word for a staff or cane. Why was that image chosen?

options.label: The first ones discovered were rod-shaped
They were first found growing on walking sticks
They were thought to hold up the plants around them
They move in a slow, stepping way across surfaces

items.explain: The word comes from the diminutive of a Greek word meaning staff or cane, because the first bacteria discovered were rod-shaped.

items.prompt: A student assumes scientists have studied bacterial species about equally. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Studies cover each named species in equal measure
Studies avoid disease-causing species because of danger
Studies pile onto a few species, mostly ones that affect health
Studies are spread out according to how common species are

items.explain: Just 10 species account for half of all publications, nearly 75% of named bacteria have no research on them, and most studies focus on pathogens relevant to human health.

steps.text: The term bacteria traditionally included all prokaryotes.
In the 1990s prokaryotes were found to consist of two very different groups, Bacteria and Archaea.
Those two groups evolved from an ancient common ancestor.
So Bacteria and Archaea must be one and the same group after all.

beats.explain: They share an ancient ancestor but are very different groups, and they are called separate evolutionary domains.

paragraphs.heading: What bacteria are
paragraphs.text: Bacteria make up a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms. Most live freely, and many consist of just one cell, typically a few micrometres long. Their cells carry circular chromosomes, have no nucleus and rarely contain membrane-bound organelles, which sets them apart from the cells of animals and other eukaryotes. Bacteria were among the first forms of life to appear on Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Everywhere on Earth
paragraphs.text: Bacteria live in the air, soil and water, in acidic hot springs, in radioactive waste and deep in Earth's crust. They are abundant in lakes, oceans and arctic ice, and they live on and inside plants and animals. There are thought to be around 2×10³⁰ of them on the planet, a biomass that only plants exceed. Each person carries roughly 10¹³ to 10¹⁴ bacteria, most of them in the gut and many on the skin.

paragraphs.heading: Recyclers of the living world
paragraphs.text: Bacteria keep nutrients moving through the nutrient cycle. They recycle nutrients and fix nitrogen taken from the atmosphere, and they carry out putrefaction, the rotting stage when dead bodies decompose. Around hydrothermal vents and cold seeps, extremophile bacteria turn dissolved compounds such as hydrogen sulphide and methane into energy, supplying the nutrients that sustain life there. People put them to work too: in sewage treatment, breaking down oil spills, making cheese and yogurt, recovering metals such as gold and copper, and making antibiotics.

paragraphs.heading: Friends and foes
paragraphs.text: Bacteria live alongside plants and animals in mutualistic, commensal and parasitic relationships. Most of the ones in and on our bodies are harmless, or are kept harmless by the immune system, and many in the gut are helpful. Several species cause infectious diseases, among them tuberculosis, cholera, leprosy, syphilis, tetanus, anthrax and bubonic plague. The most common deadly bacterial illnesses are respiratory infections. Antibiotics treat these infections but are also used in farming, and resistance to them is a growing problem.

paragraphs.heading: A deep history
paragraphs.text: The ancestors of bacteria were single-celled microorganisms that were the first forms of life on Earth, about 4 billion years ago. For about 3 billion years most life was microscopic, with bacteria and archaea in charge. In the 1990s scientists found that prokaryotes are really two very different groups, now the domains Bacteria and Archaea. Bacteria also helped build more complex cells: ancient bacteria swallowed by early eukaryotic cells became mitochondria or hydrogenosomes. Later, some of those cells swallowed cyanobacteria-like organisms, which became the chloroplasts of algae and plants.

paragraphs.heading: Mostly unknown
paragraphs.text: About 43,000 species of bacteria have been named, yet most have never been studied, and many species cannot be grown in a laboratory. Just 10 species account for half of all publications, while nearly 75% of named bacteria have no research devoted to them. Escherichia coli, the best-studied species, has more than 300,000 studies. Even so, a quarter of its 4000 genes are still poorly studied or uncharacterized.
